rv.q: Manual Cinema's Frankenstein is also a brilliant piece of theater that unapologetically celebrates the vast promise of human creativity and ingenuity.

In a very real way, in almost every way I can think of, this darkly wonderful masterpiece of “handmade puppets, practical effects, cinematic techniques, innovative sound, and original music” is just about perfect.
It is a masterwork of visual storytelling, a triumph of imagination and technique, and one of the most distinctive theatrical works to emerge from Chicago in the past decade.

Anyone ready to wipe their hands of this derivative planet should go immediately to Manual Cinema’s shadow puppetry and live film extravaganza Frankenstein , directed by Drew Dir, now at the Studebaker Theater in the Fine Arts Building.

“Frankenstein” rewards the curiosity of the audience by showing the stagecraft without it being at the expense of the story being told, like watching a reverse magician, whose tricks become even more impressive and magical when you know how they are done.

cn.t: Critics rave about Manual Cinema's Frankenstein as a breathtaking fusion of puppetry, film, and live sound design. A near-unanimous triumph, it's hailed as genuinely innovative theatrical genius.
